source.title: GP-MoLFormer: A Foundation Model For Molecular Generation
source.authors: Jerret Ross; Brian M. Belgodere; Samuel C. Hoffman; Vijil Chenthamarakshan; Jirí Navrátil; Youssef Mroueh; Payel Das

page_placements.theme: Scale changes error composition and output diversity

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses and cites language-model scaling work, but its own scaling experiments concern molecular-generation novelty, not held-out loss, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports novelty as generation-pool size increases and compares models trained on 650M versus 1.1B SMILES. These measure a different outcome from the claim versions. Scaling results attributed to other work are cited, not reproduced.
record.test_reason: No result bears on any version. The study measures novelty, validity and uniqueness of generated SMILES against generation-pool size (30k–10B), for two 46.8M models trained on 650M de-duplicated vs 1.1B raw SMILES. It reports no held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute, and no downstream-versus-scale curve. The two training sets differ in both size and duplication, so even the data comparison is confounded. Kaplan et al. and Frey et al. (chemical power-law loss) are only cited.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that training-data duplication increases memorization and lowers novelty. They also claim an inference-compute 'scaling law' relating generation count to novelty, which is an exponential decay rather than a power law. They say the model still yields significant novelty (16.7–21.4%) at 10B generations. They make no claims about loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales the number of molecular generations and measures novelty, rather than measuring held-out loss across parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Novelty differs with training-data size and deduplication status, and with generation-pool size.

fits_no_version.finding: Generation novelty stays near flat (≈0.39–0.40 Uniq; ≈0.32–0.33 raw) up to 100M generations, then falls by 10B (0.214 Uniq; 0.167 raw). The authors fit an exponential decay y = a·exp(-bx), not a power law. The de-duplicated 650M model has higher novelty at every pool size, but data size and duplication are confounded.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In large chemical language models, novelty of generations falls with inference sample count (fit as exponential decay) and rises with training-data de-duplication.

record.problems: The study does not measure held-out cross-entropy or vary parameter count, training tokens, or compute to test the stated loss laws. Its reported scaling outcome is molecular novelty, a different measure.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant table rows were omitted. Other reported measures in Table 6 (validity and uniqueness) do not measure the claim or the novelty finding catalogued here.

untested.parts: Held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; no loss values are reported.
Extrapolation of loss fits from small to large runs.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count; only one architecture (12 layers, 768 hidden) is used.
Power-law loss in a molecular-string modality; only the cited Frey et al. result addresses this, not the study's own runs.
Downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss; model size is never varied.
Dependence of fitted loss exponents or allocation on setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The 'scaling law' here is about inference sample count versus novelty, not about training loss. The text contradicts itself on which model has the higher initial value 'a': the main text says GP-MolFormer, Figure S7 says Uniq. The rows correctly carry versions ['none'] with state cannot_determine.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether loss fits from smaller runs predict much larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocation at fixed compute.
Effect of depth, width, and architecture at fixed parameter count on loss.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss exponents and compute-optimal allocation on setup or fitting choices, and departures from a single loss power law.

relation.reason: Beyond introductory citations, p. 9 substantively discusses prior chemical-model power-law loss scaling and downstream data scaling, comparing their settings and findings with this study.

tranche.reason: Generation-pool novelty and its exponential fit do not test any listed claim version. Prior results on loss and downstream scaling are cited results.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated 31 March 2025. Its exponential novelty fit against generation count is not evidence against the catalog's power-law loss claims.
